files.name: login.go

notes.2: Parses the request body and query string into form values.
notes.8: Checks the submitted credentials and returns a session on success.
notes.13: Stores the session id in a cookie that is HTTP-only and Secure.
notes.15: Reads the optional 'next' query parameter, which says where to send the user after login.
notes.16: Falls back to the default page when 'next' is missing or fails a check.
notes.19: Sends a 303 response whose Location header is the chosen target.

options.label: The Secure cookie flag stops the session cookie being set over HTTP, so the user can be tricked into logging in again.
options.whyWrong: The cookie flags are set correctly and are unrelated to where the user is redirected.

options.label: A prefix check for "/" also accepts values like "//evil.example" or "/\evil.example". Browsers read these as scheme-relative URLs pointing at another host, so the redirect after login can go to an attacker's site.
Reading 'next' from the query string instead of the POST body lets the server fetch an attacker-chosen URL from inside the network.
options.whyWrong: The server never fetches the URL. It only hands it to the browser, so this is not SSRF.

options.label: The redirect uses status 303 instead of 302, which lets the attacker replay the POST request against another site.
options.whyWrong: 303 makes the browser follow with a GET. The status code is not the problem.

options.label: Reject any 'next' value containing "://"
options.whyWrong: "//evil.example" contains no "://", so it still passes and the browser still treats it as an external host.

options.label: Parse the URL and only reject when it has a scheme
options.whyWrong: "//evil.example/x" parses with an empty scheme but a non-empty Host, so it passes this check. The check also now accepts values with no leading slash.

options.label: Also reject values starting with "//" or "/\"
Require that 'next' ends with the site's own domain
options.whyWrong: Suffix checks are easy to bypass, for example with "https://evil.example/?x=example.com" or "https://notexample.com". It also rejects normal relative paths like /dashboard.

training.exploit: An attacker sends a victim a link such as https://shop.example/login?next=//evil.example/login. The page looks genuine and the victim enters real credentials. The server authenticates them, sets the cookie, and answers with Location: //evil.example/login. The check only tests for a leading "/", so it passes. The browser reads the value as a scheme-relative URL and lands on the attacker's lookalike page, which can say 'session expired, please log in again' and capture the credentials a second time.

hints.line: Look at how the code decides that 'next' is a safe, local destination.
hints.bugClass: The user is being sent somewhere an attacker picks, and the server never fetches anything itself.
hints.why: Think about what a browser does with a Location header that starts with two slashes.
hints.fix: The fix must reject the inputs that look like local paths but resolve to another host.

writeup.summary: The login handler redirects to a user-supplied 'next' parameter after checking only that it starts with "/". Values like "//evil.example" and "/\evil.example" pass that check, but browsers resolve them as scheme-relative URLs to another host. An attacker can therefore make a genuine login page send victims to a phishing site right after they authenticate. The fix rejects values starting with "//" or "/\", so only true same-origin paths are accepted. A stricter option is to allow only paths from a known list or to map short tokens to destinations.
